items.prompt: Elena checks over 40 raw sources continuously and still ends the month unsure what's true. Diego checks one weekly digest from 3 curators and can confidently name what mattered. What is curation, as this unit uses the term?
choices: Reading faster so you can push through a larger share of the raw stream in the same amount of time
Deciding, before you read anything, which small slice of a flood of information is even worth letting reach your attention
Fact-checking one specific claim after you've already decided to read it carefully
Memorizing everything a field has ever published so nothing of substance is ever missed
items.explanation: Curation is the upstream filtering decision — what gets let in at all — not a reading-speed fix (checking faster still means checking everything), and not a downstream check on one already-chosen claim (that's evaluating a source, a separate skill). Comprehensively tracking a fast field's entire raw output isn't achievable regardless of speed.
items.reference:
The claim: Curation decides what even reaches your attention, before you read a single word.

Why: Elena read the raw stream directly (no filter); Diego let 3 trusted curators filter first — same field, ten times less time, more of it actually known.

items.prompt: How does curation differ from deciding whether one specific claim you've already chosen to read is trustworthy?
choices: They're really the same underlying skill, just applied at different times of the day
Curation is the earlier, higher-volume filter deciding what's worth attention at all; trusting one already-chosen claim happens only after something has already been let in
Curation, by definition, only applies to topics you've personally decided don't matter
Curation means accepting whatever a well-known expert says, without any further question
items.explanation: Curation happens before you're looking at any particular claim — it decides which small slice of the flood gets a look at all. Judging one specific, already-selected claim's trustworthiness is a separate, later step that curation doesn't replace.
items.reference:
The claim: Curation decides what even reaches your attention, before you read a single word.

Why: Elena read the raw stream directly (no filter); Diego let 3 trusted curators filter first — same field, ten times less time, more of it actually known.

items.prompt: Diego's three curators already read the raw 200-item weekly flood and pass along only what survived scrutiny. What role are they playing in his system?
choices: They're doing the curation step — filtering the flood down before it reaches Diego's attention at all
They're just faster readers who cover the same ground Elena covers, at the same volume
They're evaluating a single claim Diego already picked out for them
They're irrelevant — the real filtering happens when Diego reads the digest himself
items.explanation: The curators are the filtering step itself: most of the raw 200 items get dropped before Diego ever sees them. That upstream volume reduction — not anything Diego does afterward — is what curation means here.
items.reference:
The claim: Curation decides what even reaches your attention, before you read a single word.

Why: Elena read the raw stream directly (no filter); Diego let 3 trusted curators filter first — same field, ten times less time, more of it actually known.

items.prompt: Elena spent about 10 hours a week checking raw feeds; Diego spent about 1 hour a week on a batched digest. What does the outcome of their month show about the relationship between checking time and actual knowledge?
choices: More checking time reliably and directly produces more real knowledge, in proportion
More checking time can produce less real knowledge, if most of what's checked is unfiltered noise
Checking time and real knowledge turn out to be entirely unrelated in any field at all
Diego's better outcome was mostly luck and wouldn't hold up if the month were repeated
items.explanation: Elena's extra nine hours a week went into a raw, unfiltered stream — more exposure to noise, not more exposure to signal. Diego's far smaller time budget, spent on already-filtered material, produced more usable, confident knowledge. Time spent doesn't automatically convert to knowledge gained; what you spend it reading does.
items.reference:
The claim: Constant checking costs real time and attention, and that cost doesn't buy proportionally more real knowledge.

Why: Elena spent ~10x Diego's hours and ended up less sure of what was true, not more.

items.prompt: Why did Elena end the month less confident about what was true, despite spending far more time than Diego?
choices: Because she is, in general, a noticeably less careful reader than Diego is
Because most of her ten hours went into raw, unfiltered claims — several of which later turned out to be overstated — leaving her with a jumble to sort out rather than confirmed knowledge
Because nutrition science happens to be an unusually unpredictable field compared to most others
Because she did most of her checking in the mornings rather than in the evenings
items.explanation: The confusion came from volume without filtering: four of the five claims she chased and acted on fizzled, leaving her to untangle which of five things she half-believed was actually still true. Diego's smaller, pre-filtered set never included the fizzles in the first place.
items.reference:
The claim: Constant checking costs real time and attention, and that cost doesn't buy proportionally more real knowledge.

Why: Elena spent ~10x Diego's hours and ended up less sure of what was true, not more.

items.prompt: "I have a bit of downtime, it doesn't hurt to check the raw feed one more time today" — what's the flaw in that reasoning, per this unit?
choices: There's no real flaw here — any extra checking is a pure bonus whenever the time exists
It treats checking time as free just because it's available, ignoring that in a fast field, more raw checking mostly adds noise rather than converting into more real knowledge
Checking during downtime is perfectly fine, but only when it's done before noon
The flaw described here is only relevant if you happen to follow fewer than ten sources
items.explanation: Having spare time doesn't change what an extra raw-feed check actually returns: in a fast field, most of the incremental material is noise, not signal, so 'I have the time' doesn't turn extra checking into extra real knowledge the way it might feel like it should.
items.reference:
The claim: Constant checking costs real time and attention, and that cost doesn't buy proportionally more real knowledge.

Why: Elena spent ~10x Diego's hours and ended up less sure of what was true, not more.

items.prompt: What is the key structural difference between Elena's approach and Diego's approach to the same fast-moving field?
choices: Elena reads the raw, unfiltered stream directly from 40+ sources; Diego reads a small set of trusted curators who have already filtered that same stream
Elena simply reads more carefully, sentence by sentence, than Diego does each week
Diego's approach means he avoids engaging with the field's real information almost entirely
There is no real structural difference — both end up seeing the same material, just at different times
items.explanation: Elena's sources are raw and unfiltered — nothing stands between the flood and her attention. Diego's three curators sit between him and that same flood, already having dropped most of it before he ever sees a digest.
items.reference:
The claim: A raw firehose (many unfiltered sources) and a small set of trusted filters are two different strategies for the same problem — staying current in a fast field.

Why: Elena followed 40+ sources directly; Diego followed 3 curators who already filtered the same field for him.

items.prompt: Diego never sees the four claims that fizzled during the month, while Elena saw and acted on all five. What does that difference show about what a trusted filter does?
choices: A trusted filter mainly speeds up how quickly you see new claims
A trusted filter reduces the actual volume of what reaches you, not just when it arrives
A trusted filter guarantees that every claim it lets through is true
A trusted filter has no measurable effect on which claims you end up seeing
items.explanation: The four fizzled claims simply never appeared in Diego's digest — they were dropped, not delayed. A trusted filter's main value is that volume reduction: most of the raw material never reaches you at all, not just that it reaches you a bit later.
items.reference:
The claim: A raw firehose (many unfiltered sources) and a small set of trusted filters are two different strategies for the same problem — staying current in a fast field.

Why: Elena followed 40+ sources directly; Diego followed 3 curators who already filtered the same field for him.

items.prompt: Diego reviews his digest once a week, in one sitting. What is this practice called in this unit, and what does it replace?
choices: Batching — it replaces checking continuously throughout the day
Skimming — it replaces reading anything in full
Curating — it replaces trusting any source at all
Archiving — it replaces ever revisiting older claims
items.explanation: Batching means reviewing new information on a fixed schedule instead of checking continuously. It's a separate habit from curation itself (which decides what gets filtered), but the two work together in Diego's system.
items.reference:
The claim: Reviewing on a fixed batch schedule, instead of checking continuously, is part of what makes a curation system work.

Why: Diego reviews once a week in one sitting; Elena checks continuously throughout the day.

items.prompt: Elena checks her raw feeds six to eight times a day. What does batching (Diego's approach) change about that pattern, specifically?
choices: It reduces the actual number of sources Diego follows down to zero over time
It replaces frequent, scattered checking throughout the day with one review on a fixed schedule
It requires Diego to check even more often than Elena does, just using better sources
It has essentially nothing to do with how often you check — only with what you read
items.explanation: Batching is specifically about frequency and timing of review, not about source quality (that's curation). Diego's one-sitting weekly review is the batching half of his system, distinct from — but complementary to — his three trusted curators.
items.reference:
The claim: Reviewing on a fixed batch schedule, instead of checking continuously, is part of what makes a curation system work.

Why: Diego reviews once a week in one sitting; Elena checks continuously throughout the day.

items.prompt: Why does this unit argue for a deliberate "good enough, move on" threshold instead of trying to be comprehensively current in a fast-moving field?
choices: Because comprehensive currency is technically achievable but simply not worth the effort

Because in a genuinely fast field, the volume produced outpaces any reading pace, so comprehensive currency isn't actually achievable — chasing it just produces more checking without more real knowledge
Because a good-enough threshold means you should stop learning about the field entirely after just one review
Because curators always disagree with each other, so real certainty is impossible no matter the effort
items.explanation: The field's volume grows faster than anyone can read it — that's structural, not a personal shortcoming. A 'good enough' threshold accepts that and stops chasing full coverage; trying to be comprehensively current, as Elena did, just means more time spent without closing the gap.
items.reference:
The claim: A deliberate "good enough, move on" threshold beats trying to be comprehensively current.

Why: In a genuinely fast field, full comprehensive currency isn't achievable — chasing it is what drove Elena's ten hours a week.

items.prompt: Diego stops at one weekly digest and doesn't try to also skim the raw feeds "just in case" his curators missed something. Is this consistent with the good-enough threshold described in this unit?
choices: No — a genuinely careful, thorough person should always double-check the raw feeds too
Yes — deliberately stopping at a level of currency that's sufficient for his purposes, rather than chasing full comprehensive coverage, is exactly what the threshold means
No — this kind of threshold only applies to topics that don't matter to the reader at all
Yes, but only because Diego doesn't actually care very much about this field
items.explanation: Stopping at a level that's sufficient, on purpose, rather than continuing to chase full coverage, is the good-enough threshold in action. It's not indifference — Diego clearly cares enough to review weekly — it's a deliberate limit on how far that effort goes.
items.reference:
The claim: A deliberate "good enough, move on" threshold beats trying to be comprehensively current.

Why: In a genuinely fast field, full comprehensive currency isn't achievable — chasing it is what drove Elena's ten hours a week.

items.prompt: A colleague says: "I'll never really be caught up in this field, so what's the point of even trying to filter what I read?" How does this unit's good-enough threshold respond to that framing?
choices: It agrees with the framing — since full currency is impossible, filtering is ultimately pointless
It reframes the goal: the point isn't reaching full currency (impossible in a genuinely fast field), it's reaching a deliberately chosen, sufficient level of currency with far less time and noise
It suggests the colleague should instead try reading even more broadly to compensate for the gap
It says filtering only really starts to matter once you're already an expert in that field
items.explanation: The good-enough threshold doesn't chase an impossible goal (full currency) — it replaces that goal with a deliberately chosen, sufficient one. Giving up on filtering because full currency is unreachable throws away the actual achievable win: much less time spent, and more of what you do know being reliable.
items.reference:
The claim: A deliberate "good enough, move on" threshold beats trying to be comprehensively current.

Why: In a genuinely fast field, full comprehensive currency isn't achievable — chasing it is what drove Elena's ten hours a week.

items.prompt: In a genuinely fast-moving field, why doesn't checking more often get you closer to feeling 'caught up'?
choices: Because checking more often always makes a person feel more anxious, no matter the field
Because the volume of material a fast field produces grows faster than any reading pace can match, so the gap between what's produced and what's read doesn't close
Because 'caught up' turns out to be a basically meaningless phrase in any field at all
Because most fields eventually slow down on their own, if you're just willing to wait long enough
items.explanation: The core mismatch is structural: attention is a small, fixed budget, while a fast field's volume is effectively unbounded. Reading more often just spends that fixed budget faster on whatever's loudest at the moment — it doesn't shrink the gap, because the gap is set by volume outpacing attention, not by checking frequency.
items.reference:
The claim: Attention is a small, fixed budget; volume in a fast field is effectively unbounded — checking more doesn't close that gap.

Why: A fast field's output grows faster than any reading pace could match, so 'caught up' isn't reachable by reading harder.

items.prompt: Elena's strategy was to read more of the raw stream to try to keep up. According to the volume-vs-attention model, what's the actual problem with that strategy?
choices: It applies a strategy (read more) to a problem (unbounded volume vs. fixed attention) that more reading structurally can't solve
It's basically a fine strategy, just one that was poorly executed in her specific case
It would have worked fine if she had simply read roughly twice as fast as she did
The problem described here only applies to nutrition science, not to other fast-moving fields
items.explanation: Reading faster or more often doesn't change the structural mismatch between fixed attention and effectively unbounded volume — it's the same losing race run slightly faster. The fix has to change what reaches her attention in the first place (filtering), not how quickly she processes what's already reaching her.
items.reference:
The claim: Attention is a small, fixed budget; volume in a fast field is effectively unbounded — checking more doesn't close that gap.

Why: A fast field's output grows faster than any reading pace could match, so 'caught up' isn't reachable by reading harder.

items.prompt: As a fast-moving field grows in output over time (more publications, more accounts, more takes), what happens to the gap between volume and any one person's fixed attention?
choices: The gap shrinks automatically as more curators emerge to cover it
The gap widens, since attention stays roughly fixed while volume keeps growing
The gap stays exactly the same regardless of how much the field grows
The gap only matters for fields with fewer than 10 active sources
items.explanation: Attention doesn't scale up the way a field's output can — so as volume grows, the mismatch between what's produced and what one person can absorb widens, not narrows. That's exactly why filtering harder, not reading harder, is the fix this unit argues for.
items.reference:
The claim: Attention is a small, fixed budget; volume in a fast field is effectively unbounded — checking more doesn't close that gap.

Why: A fast field's output grows faster than any reading pace could match, so 'caught up' isn't reachable by reading harder.

items.prompt: The funnel model has three stages: raw stream, trusted filters, batched review. What does the 'trusted filters' stage actually do to the raw stream, according to this unit?
choices: It relays the entire raw stream unchanged, just organized into one place
It drops most of the raw stream and only lets through what survives some scrutiny
It adds new claims that weren't in the raw stream at all
It slows down the raw stream without changing its volume
items.explanation: The filter stage's main job is volume reduction: most raw items are dropped entirely, not merely relayed later. What reaches the batched-review stage is a smaller, different set than the raw stream — not the same set on a delay.
items.reference:
The claim: A curation funnel drops most of the raw stream and adds a scrutiny delay before anything reaches you.

Why: Trusted filters don't just relay the same raw stream later — they drop most of it, so what reaches you is a smaller, different set.

items.prompt: Someone argues that trusted curators are just a slower way of seeing the exact same information Elena sees directly, so there's no real benefit besides a delay. What does this unit say is wrong with that framing?
choices: It's correct — a curator system really is purely a delay mechanism with no volume effect at all
It's wrong — the filter stage drops most raw items outright, so a curated reader sees a smaller, different set of claims, not the same set later
It's wrong, but mainly because curators sometimes introduce extra false information of their own
It's correct, but the delay by itself is still valuable enough on its own to matter
items.explanation: The delay enables the drop (there's no way to sort signal from hype the instant something's published), but the drop itself — most raw items never reaching the reader at all — is the actual mechanism, not just a lag on identical content.
items.reference:
The claim: A curation funnel drops most of the raw stream and adds a scrutiny delay before anything reaches you.

Why: Trusted filters don't just relay the same raw stream later — they drop most of it, so what reaches you is a smaller, different set.

items.prompt: What does the 'recency bias check' heuristic warn against?
choices: Trusting anything at all that was published more than a month ago
Treating a claim as more significant simply because it's newer, rather than asking whether it's actually more significant on its own merits
Reading new information at all, regardless of where it comes from or who wrote it
Following more than three separate sources within any single fast-moving field
items.explanation: The heuristic isn't anti-new-information — it's against equating 'new' with 'important.' A fast field always has a steady stream of new items; if newness alone drove attention, you'd chase whatever showed up most recently regardless of substance.
items.reference:
The claim: Newness isn't automatically significance — ask whether a claim actually matters more, not just whether it's more recent.

Why: A steady stream of new items exists in any fast field; treating 'new' as 'important' guarantees chasing whatever showed up today.

items.prompt: Why does the recency bias heuristic matter specifically in a fast-moving field, more than in a slow one?
choices: Because fast fields have a constant supply of new items, so 'this is new' stops being a useful signal of importance by itself — something is always new
Because slow-moving fields, by contrast, essentially never produce anything genuinely new
Because recency bias, as a pattern, only really exists in fields related to health and science
Because fast fields simply have fewer sources available to choose from overall
items.explanation: In a fast field, there's always something new — so 'new' can't do the work of distinguishing what matters, since practically everything qualifies. The heuristic pushes past newness to ask about actual significance instead.
items.reference:
The claim: Newness isn't automatically significance — ask whether a claim actually matters more, not just whether it's more recent.

Why: A steady stream of new items exists in any fast field; treating 'new' as 'important' guarantees chasing whatever showed up today.

items.prompt: A curator writes: 'This just came out today, so it's the most important development this month.' What's the flaw in that reasoning, per the recency heuristic?
choices: There's no real flaw — today's news is, by definition, always the most important item
It substitutes recency for significance — being the newest item doesn't establish that it's actually the most important one
The only real flaw is that the curator should have waited a full year before commenting
The flaw is simply that curators should never comment on same-day news at all
items.explanation: Calling something the most important development purely because it's the newest one conflates two different properties. The recency heuristic asks for evidence of actual significance, independent of how recently the claim appeared.
items.reference:
The claim: Newness isn't automatically significance — ask whether a claim actually matters more, not just whether it's more recent.

Why: A steady stream of new items exists in any fast field; treating 'new' as 'important' guarantees chasing whatever showed up today.

items.prompt: What does 'regression to the mean' predict about the loudest, most dramatic early claims in a fast field?
choices: That they are usually the most accurate claims available, since drama tends to reflect genuine importance
That they tend, on average, to moderate toward something less extreme as more evidence and replication come in
That they should be permanently ignored the moment they're identified as dramatic
That this pattern only applies to claims that come from anonymous, unnamed sources
items.explanation: Regression to the mean predicts that extreme early framings tend to moderate over time as more careful evidence accumulates — not that they're automatically wrong, but that the odds favor a less dramatic eventual picture than the loudest early version suggested.
items.reference:
The claim: The loudest early claims are, on average, overstated — they tend to moderate as more evidence comes in.

Why: Early reports are more likely to come from whoever framed a result most dramatically, not whoever assessed it most carefully.

items.prompt: Why are the loudest early claims about a new finding more likely to be overstated, according to this unit's reasoning?
choices: Because early reporters covering a new finding are, as a rule, usually being dishonest
Because early reports are more likely to come from whoever framed the result most dramatically, not from whoever assessed it most carefully
Because dramatic framing of new findings is, in effect, legally required to be exaggerated
Because early claims about anything are always made by first-time sources with no prior track record
items.explanation: The mechanism isn't dishonesty — it's a selection effect. The most attention-grabbing framing of a new result tends to spread fastest and loudest early on, before more careful, less dramatic assessments have had time to catch up and moderate the picture.
items.reference:
The claim: The loudest early claims are, on average, overstated — they tend to moderate as more evidence comes in.

Why: Early reports are more likely to come from whoever framed a result most dramatically, not whoever assessed it most carefully.

items.prompt: Why does this unit weight sources by track record rather than by how confident or fluent they sound?
choices: Because confidence and fluency happen to be reliable signals of accuracy in any fast field
Confidence and fluency are cheap for a source to produce regardless of whether it's right, while an actual track record of past calls holding up is expensive to fake
Because track record, as a signal, only really matters for sources with over 1,000 followers
Because fluent, polished writing always correlates with a source having done more real research
items.explanation: Anyone can sound confident and write fluently, whether or not the underlying claim holds up — that signal is nearly free to produce. A track record of previously-right calls, built up over real time, is much harder to fake, which is why it's the more reliable weighting criterion.
items.reference:
The claim: Weight a source by whether its past 'this matters' calls actually held up, not by how confident it sounds right now.

Why: Confidence and fluency are cheap to fake; a track record of being right before is expensive to fake.

items.prompt: Two sources both make a confident, dramatic new claim. Source A has repeatedly been right about similar claims before; Source B is brand new with no history either way. What does the track-record heuristic suggest about weighting these two claims?
choices: Weight them both identically, since each source sounds equally confident about its claim
Weight Source A's claim more heavily than Source B's, based on A's demonstrated history of being right, not on how confidently either one states it
Weight Source B's claim more heavily instead, since genuinely new sources tend to be more trustworthy
Ignore both claims entirely, since neither has yet been independently replicated by anyone
items.explanation: Confidence is the same for both, so it can't be the deciding factor — the track-record heuristic says to lean on A's demonstrated history instead. That doesn't mean automatically dismissing B, but B's claim should sit with less weight until it either gets independent confirmation or B builds a track record of its own.
items.reference:
The claim: Weight a source by whether its past 'this matters' calls actually held up, not by how confident it sounds right now.

Why: Confidence and fluency are cheap to fake; a track record of being right before is expensive to fake.

items.prompt: A curator has been consistently right about which early claims later held up, across many past calls. What does the track-record heuristic say this history is worth?
choices: Nothing at all — past accuracy has no real bearing on whether a new claim from that source is trustworthy
It's worth real weight — a consistent history of being right before is expensive to fake and a meaningful signal for weighting the source's current claims
It only really matters if the curator in question also happens to have the most followers
It's worth less, in practice, than how confident the source's tone sounds in a specific post
items.explanation: A demonstrated history of accurate calls is exactly what the track-record heuristic treats as valuable — it's hard to fake over time, unlike confidence or fluency, which makes it a genuinely useful (though not infallible) input into how much weight to give a source's current claim.
items.reference:
The claim: Weight a source by whether its past 'this matters' calls actually held up, not by how confident it sounds right now.

Why: Confidence and fluency are cheap to fake; a track record of being right before is expensive to fake.

items.prompt: Of the roughly 200 raw items published in Diego's example week, only two turned out to be genuinely new pieces of information. What happened to the rest, and where?
choices: Diego personally read through all 200 himself and decided individually which ones to ignore
Most were dropped upstream, before Diego's review, because they were duplicate coverage, pure opinion with no new evidence, or already-flagged engagement bait
The other 198 items were simply saved aside and carried over for review the following week
The other 198 items actually turned out to be more important than the two the digest flagged
items.explanation: The volume reduction happens at the filter stage, not in Diego's own hour of review — his curators dropped nearly all 200 items before the digest ever reached him, because they added no new information beyond what was already covered or flagged.
items.reference:
The claim: Most of a week's raw flood gets dropped upstream, before any per-item judgment is needed from the reader.

Why: Of ~200 raw items in Diego's week, only 2 were genuinely new information — everything else was duplicate coverage, pure opinion, or already-flagged engagement bait.

items.prompt: Why does it matter that the raw flood gets reduced before Diego's own review, rather than him personally deciding item-by-item what to skip?
choices: It doesn't really matter either way — the total time spent ends up roughly the same

It matters because per-item judgment on 200 items would itself consume far more time and attention than the one hour Diego actually spends — the funnel's value is removing that burden entirely, not just making it faster
It matters mainly because Diego personally dislikes having to make decisions of this kind
It matters because curators are, under some formal arrangement, legally required to pre-filter content
items.explanation: If Diego had to individually evaluate all 200 raw items, he'd be back to something like Elena's time cost. The funnel's real value is that most items never require his judgment at all — they're dropped before reaching him, which is what makes the one-hour weekly review possible.
items.reference:
The claim: Most of a week's raw flood gets dropped upstream, before any per-item judgment is needed from the reader.

Why: Of ~200 raw items in Diego's week, only 2 were genuinely new information — everything else was duplicate coverage, pure opinion, or already-flagged engagement bait.

items.prompt: In the worked week, which two items out of roughly 200 raw posts made it into Diego's digest as genuinely new information?
choices: A retraction of an old recommendation and a debate recap with no new information
The fiber and gut-health study, and the supplement pre-print claiming anti-aging effects
Six opinion pieces reacting to the same underlying study
All 15 posts that used the phrase 'new study shows'
items.explanation: The fiber study and the supplement pre-print were the only two items in the entire week's raw output that represented genuinely new information — everything else was duplicate coverage, reaction pieces, or previously-flagged material with nothing new added.
items.reference:
The claim: Most of a week's raw flood gets dropped upstream, before any per-item judgment is needed from the reader.

Why: Of ~200 raw items in Diego's week, only 2 were genuinely new information — everything else was duplicate coverage, pure opinion, or already-flagged engagement bait.

items.prompt: The fiber and gut-health study was flagged 'consistent with three prior studies' and wasn't the loudest item in Diego's digest. Why did Diego treat it as the week's genuine signal despite being less exciting than the supplement claim?
choices: Because Diego, as a rule, always trusts whichever claim happens to be least exciting, regardless of evidence

Because a claim backed by a track-record source and consistent with multiple independent prior studies is stronger evidence than one dramatic, unreplicated single study, even though it's less attention-grabbing
Because fiber studies, as a category, are inherently more trustworthy than supplement studies in general
Because the supplement claim had actually already been proven false by the time Diego reviewed the digest
items.explanation: Consistency across multiple independent studies, from sources with a track record of being right, is exactly the profile the track-record and regression heuristics predict is more reliable — even though it sounds far more boring than a single dramatic new claim.
items.reference:
The claim: A claim consistent with multiple prior independent studies, from a track-record source, is stronger signal than one dramatic new single-study claim — even though it sounds far less exciting.

Why: The fiber study was flagged 'consistent with three prior studies' and confirmed months later at population scale; the supplement claim was one unreplicated study with an implausibly large effect.

items.prompt: Two months after Diego acted on the fiber study, a larger meta-analysis confirmed the finding at population scale. What does this outcome illustrate about the heuristics from L2?
choices: That dramatic, single-study claims are, in general, usually more reliable than the model predicts

That a claim's consistency across multiple prior studies and a track-record source was, in this case, a genuinely useful signal for identifying real, durable findings before comprehensive confirmation arrived
That Diego simply got lucky here and the heuristics from L2 played no real role at all
That waiting for a full meta-analysis is always strictly necessary before acting on anything
items.explanation: The fiber study's eventual confirmation is exactly the outcome the heuristics were designed to anticipate: signals with a track record and prior consistency behind them are more likely to hold up than they might seem relative to louder, newer claims — which is what let Diego act with real confidence weeks before broader confirmation existed.
items.reference:
The claim: A claim consistent with multiple prior independent studies, from a track-record source, is stronger signal than one dramatic new single-study claim — even though it sounds far less exciting.

Why: The fiber study was flagged 'consistent with three prior studies' and confirmed months later at population scale; the supplement claim was one unreplicated study with an implausibly large effect.

items.prompt: Why is 'this is consistent with three prior studies' a stronger form of signal than 'this is one brand-new dramatic study,' according to the worked example?
choices: Because studies described as 'prior' are automatically considered more prestigious than brand-new ones
Because consistency across multiple independent studies, over time, is much harder to produce by chance or by an isolated framing choice than a single new dramatic result is
Because studies labeled 'prior' always happen to use larger sample sizes than newer ones
Because Diego, personally, simply prefers studies that took longer to make it to publication
items.explanation: A single dramatic new result can come from an unusual sample, an extreme framing, or plain chance. Multiple independent studies landing on the same conclusion over time is much harder to produce by any of those routes — that repeated agreement is the actual source of its strength as signal.
items.reference:
The claim: A claim consistent with multiple prior independent studies, from a track-record source, is stronger signal than one dramatic new single-study claim — even though it sounds far less exciting.

Why: The fiber study was flagged 'consistent with three prior studies' and confirmed months later at population scale; the supplement claim was one unreplicated study with an implausibly large effect.

items.prompt: A curator Diego trusts retracts a two-month-old recommendation after a larger follow-up study contradicted it. What does this unit say this retraction shows about Diego's curation system?
choices: That the whole system has completely failed and Diego should go back to reading the raw stream directly
That even a trusted-filter system with a good track record can still be fooled sometimes — a track record means right most of the time, not every time
